document_summary: Post-mortem analysis of a SEV-1 Claims Gateway outage on March 12, 2024, caused by connection pool exhaustion when processing an abnormally large batch of institutional claims, including root cause analysis, timeline, impact, and action items.

entities.name: HikariCP
entities.description: JDBC connection pool library used by Claims Gateway for PostgreSQL connections
entities.overview: HikariCP is the connection pooling library used by the Claims Gateway to manage database connections to PostgreSQL. The pool was configured with a maximum of 100 connections at the time of the March 2024 incident.
entities.details: HikariCP manages the database connection pool for the Claims Gateway, configured with a maximum of 100 connections to the Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance claims-gw-prod-01. The library provides connection pooling capabilities but was not configured with separate pools for batch vs real-time processing, which led to the March 2024 outage when a large batch exhausted all connections. The configuration was later changed in Q3 2024 when the system moved to PgBouncer connection pooling.

entities.name: claims-gw-prod-01
entities.description: Production Cloud SQL PostgreSQL database instance for Claims Gateway
entities.overview: The production PostgreSQL database instance hosted on Google Cloud SQL that serves as the primary data store for the Claims Gateway. This instance was the target of the connection pool exhaustion during the March 2024 incident.
entities.details: claims-gw-prod-01 is the Cloud SQL PostgreSQL database instance that stores Claims Gateway data. During the March 2024 incident, this database became inaccessible when the HikariCP connection pool was exhausted by the large batch of institutional claims processing. The database itself was not the problem - it was the connection pool management that caused the outage. All 100 connections in the pool were active running INSERT statements for institutional claims batch processing.

entities.name: HikariCP Pool Exhaustion Event
entities.description: Event that occurs when the Claims Gateway connection pool reaches its maximum capacity and can't serve new requests
entities.overview: This event represents the condition where the HikariCP connection pool becomes fully utilized and cannot allocate new database connections. When this happens, the Claims Gateway begins returning 503 errors and all claims processing stops.
entities.details: The HikariCP pool exhaustion event occurs when all available database connections in the pool are in use, preventing new database operations from proceeding. During the March 2024 incident, this happened when 14,000 institutional claims were processed simultaneously, each acquiring a database connection for INSERT operations. The event has cascading effects - it causes the Claims Gateway to return 503 errors, stops all claims processing (both real-time and batch), and can trigger cascading failures in downstream services like the Eligibility Service when they timeout waiting for responses from the gateway.

entities.name: Eligibility Service Timeout Cascade
entities.description: Cascading failure event where Eligibility Service's connection pool fills up due to timeouts from Claims Gateway
entities.overview: When Claims Gateway fails and stops responding, the Eligibility Service experiences timeout errors on synchronous calls from the gateway. These timeouts cause the Eligibility Service's own connection pool to fill up, creating a cascading failure.
entities.details: This cascading failure occurs because the Eligibility Service receives synchronous calls from the Claims Gateway during claim intake processing. When the Claims Gateway is failing (such as during connection pool exhaustion), these calls timeout but still consume connection pool resources in the Eligibility Service while waiting. The accumulation of these hanging connections eventually fills up the Eligibility Service's connection pool, causing it to also become unavailable. This demonstrates the lack of circuit breaker patterns between the services, which was identified as a preventive action item (CLV-3904) but was later deprioritized.

relationships.reasoning: Gateway connection pool exhaustion causes timeouts that cascade to Eligibility Service
This cascading failure directly impacts Eligibility Service availability

entities.name: Claims Gateway Incident Response
entities.description: The operational process followed during the March 2024 Claims Gateway outage
entities.overview: This incident response process involved detecting the outage through Datadog alerts, initial misdiagnosis as a network issue, escalation to bring in additional expertise, root cause identification, and systematic resolution steps.
entities.details: The incident response process began at 02:43 UTC when a Datadog alert fired for error rate exceeding 50%. The on-call engineer (Marcus Reeves) initially misdiagnosed the issue as a network problem based on generic timeout error messages and attempted resolution by restarting gateway pods at 02:55. When this provided only temporary relief, Priya Anand was escalated at 03:10 and identified the actual root cause using pg_stat_activity to see all 100 connections running INSERT statements. The systematic resolution involved: 1) killing the batch processing job, 2) restarting gateway pods, 3) restoring professional claims processing, 4) resubmitting the institutional batch in smaller 500-claim chunks, and 5) verification of complete processing. The process revealed gaps in alerting, error messaging clarity, and architectural separation of concerns.

entities.name: Batch vs Real-time Connection Separation
entities.description: Architectural pattern requiring separate connection pools for batch and real-time processing
entities.overview: This design principle requires that batch operations and real-time operations use separate database connection pools to prevent batch processing from starving real-time operations of database connections.
entities.details: This architectural pattern addresses the fundamental conflict between batch processing (which can consume many connections for extended periods) and real-time processing (which requires guaranteed connection availability for low-latency responses). The March 2024 incident demonstrated the risks when this separation doesn't exist - a large batch of 14,000 institutional claims exhausted all 100 connections in the shared pool, preventing real-time professional claims from being processed and violating the 30-second SLA. The lack of this separation was identified as a known design issue that was deprioritized in Q4 2023 but became critical after the incident. Implementation was completed in sprint 38 (CLV-3901) with separate connection pools for batch and real-time processing.

entities.name: Batch Size Admission Control
entities.description: Business rule limiting the maximum number of claims that can be submitted in a single batch
entities.overview: This rule caps batch submissions at 2,000 claims per batch to prevent resource exhaustion. Large submissions must be split into multiple smaller batches.
entities.details: The batch size admission control rule was implemented after the March 2024 incident where Northeast Clearinghouse submitted an abnormally large batch of 14,000 institutional claims, far exceeding their normal 2,000-3,000 claim batches. The rule sets a hard limit of 2,000 claims per batch at the Claims Submission API /claims/batch endpoint. This prevents single large batches from overwhelming system resources, particularly database connection pools. Submitters requiring larger volumes must split their submissions into multiple 2,000-claim batches. The rule was implemented as CLV-3902 and completed by March 25, 2024. Northeast Clearinghouse was specifically notified about this new limit and adjusted their submission process accordingly.

This was identified as a known design issue that had been deprioritized in Q4 2023 but became critical after the incident. The work was completed and merged on April 2, 2024.

entities.name: CLV-3902
entities.description: Action item to add batch size limit to Claims Submission API
entities.overview: CLV-3902 was an action item to implement a 2,000 claim limit on the /claims/batch endpoint to prevent resource exhaustion from overly large batch submissions.
entities.details: CLV-3902 addressed the need for admission control on batch size following the March 2024 incident where a 14,000 claim batch overwhelmed the system. The action item added validation to the Claims Submission API's /claims/batch endpoint to reject batches larger than 2,000 claims. This forces large submissions to be split into manageable chunks. The work was completed and merged on March 25, 2024, making it one of the first remediation items completed after the incident.

entities.name: CLV-3905
entities.description: Action item to improve error logging for connection pool exhaustion
entities.overview: CLV-3905 improved error messages to include connection pool statistics when database connection issues occur, making diagnosis easier for on-call engineers.
entities.details: CLV-3905 addressed the diagnostic challenge identified during the March 2024 incident where the on-call engineer initially misdiagnosed the problem because error messages were generic ('Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms'). The action item enhanced error logging to include connection pool utilization statistics and clearer indicators of connection pool exhaustion. This improvement helps on-call engineers quickly identify connection pool issues rather than assuming network problems. The work was completed and merged on March 20, 2024.

entities.name: Connection Pool Utilization Alerting
entities.description: Alert threshold rule triggering when database connection pool utilization exceeds 90% for 2 minutes
entities.overview: This alerting rule monitors database connection pool utilization and triggers alerts when usage exceeds 90% for a sustained 2-minute period, providing earlier detection of connection pool exhaustion than error-rate based alerts.
entities.details: The connection pool utilization alerting rule was implemented as CLV-3903 after the March 2024 incident revealed that error-rate based alerts (50% error rate for 5 minutes) were too slow to detect connection pool exhaustion. The new rule monitors pool utilization in real-time and triggers alerts at >90% utilization sustained for 2 minutes, providing approximately 24 minutes earlier detection than the previous error-rate threshold. This proactive alerting allows operations teams to take preventive action before complete pool exhaustion occurs, such as scaling connection pools or throttling batch operations. The rule was implemented in Datadog and completed by March 19, 2024.
